newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: No change in N. Korea nuclear freeze -- IAEA.
newsitem.headline: No change in N. Korea nuclear freeze -- IAEA.

text.p: North Korea has made no move to end a freeze on its nuclear programme and is sticking to a 1994 nuclear pact with the United States, the United Nations atomic watchdog agency said on Tuesday.

The Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which has three to four experts permanently based near North Korean nuclear installations, said Pyongyang was cooperating normally with its inspectors.
"There is no change in the status quo," IAEA chief spokesman David Kyd told Reuters. "Our inspectors report that everything is normal."
North Korea signalled its frustration last week over the pace of work to replace its Soviet-designed graphite-moderated nuclear reactors with safer light-water plants.
Pyongyang's communist government agreed in a pact with Washington in 1994 to halt its nuclear plant-building programme in exchange for the provision of light-water models.
Light-water reactors produce less of the plutonium the West feared North Korea was using to develop a nuclear bomb.

An IAEA report in 1993 said some plutonium from North Korea's civil nuclear programme could not be accounted for, raising suspicions that the radioactive material was being diverted into a secret plan to construct a nuclear device.
Pyongyang said last Friday that the 1994 deal was in jeopardy because Washington was dragging its feet in implementing the accord.

"We cannot keep the nuclear programme frozen any longer only to get heavy oil, the shipments of which may be suspended any time, with no importance given to when light-water reactors will be provided," Pyongyang's official Korean News Agency (KCNA) said.

Implementation of the $4.5 billion deal to install new reactors is being carried out by the Korean Energy Development Organisation (KEDO), which includes the United States, Japan and South Korea. The European Union is to join the group once its membership and financial contributions are determined.
KEDO also agreed to provide North Korea with heavy oil shipments as an alternative source of energy until the new reactors are fully operational, perhaps in seven years' time.

IAEA experts, allowed to make regular inspections of the mothballed nuclear installations mainly based in Yongbyong, would be the first to detect any change in North Korea's compliance with the agreement.
"If there were any changes, we would inform the KEDO consortium immediately," the IAEA's Kyd said.
Diplomatic sources in Vienna said a rise in tension in North Korea was palpable after a North Korean submarine ran aground on a beach in South Korea in September.
South Korean forces killed 24 of the 26 seamen on board the submarine. One was captured and the other is still missing.

"The situation has been rather tense since the submarine affair. But the various people who take an interest in the (nuclear) issue are trying to keep matters under control," one diplomatic source said.
"There's a lot at stake here," he added.
